<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it. Here's my understanding, then my assessment.

## What the report claims

**Varden case-processing offices, 24 months, randomised:**
- The per-hour gain declined but persisted:
  - timesheet measure: +12.5% at 9 months, +9.8% at 24 months;
  - new system-log measure: +8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8).
- Output per FTE was −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2).
- Quality was unchanged, and sick days and resignations stayed lower.
- A mediation analysis registered at month 11 attributes the per-hour gain as follows:

| Pathway | Share of gain |
|---|---|
| Meetings | 47% |
| Fatigue | 18% |
| Unexplained | 35% |

**Varden counter arm:** the county ended it at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control, and restoring service would have needed 12% more staff at about 9% higher cost per contact.

**An unplanned observation:** two control offices cut meetings on their own initiative at month 15. Their output per hour then rose 4.1% against their own prior period. The authors suggest this is a hint, not a finding.

**Halden subset:** 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded.
- Three reverted. All had coverage or client obligations, and their output indices were 88–91 when they reverted.
- The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour. The authors treat this as an upper bound for self-selected survivors.

**Bearing on earlier papers:**
- The "entirely an artifact" claim fails under the very standards the re-analysis recommended.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on four long-follow-up studies that were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

## Verdict

This is a strong report, and it settles two of the open questions from my last summary.

- **It goes to the source.** It checked the meta-analysis's supplementary table, which confirms the survivorship and design concern I raised about the duration analysis.
- **It uses the better design.** The mediation test was registered before the outcome data existed.
- **It reports both measures.** Both hours measures appear, and the like-for-like comparison is the one used to assess decline.
- **It calibrates its claims.** The Halden subset and the control-office observation are both explicitly held light.

The arithmetic checks:

| Check | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Varden, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Varden, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden subset hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% |
| Halden subset per hour | 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 |

The issues below are mostly about interpretation. The first could change the size of the estimated decline.

## Issues, in order of weight

**1. The control-office meeting audit may account for part of the "decline."**
The DiD estimate is treated relative to control. If two of the seven control offices raised their output per hour by about 4% from month 15, the control baseline rose and the treated–control gap narrowed. That narrowing would happen even if treated offices didn't change at all.

As a rough calculation, weighting offices equally:
- 2 of 7 offices at +4.1% lifts the control mean by about 1.2%;
- that applies over roughly the last nine months.

That could account for perhaps a third to a half of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. The report treats the decline as "consistent with some fading of an initial effect" and treats the audit as a separate curiosity. The two need to be connected.

The fix is straightforward:
- report the treated arm's own trajectory alongside the DiD;
- re-estimate excluding the two audited control offices, as a sensitivity check.

The direction matters. Some of the apparent decay may be the control arm catching up through reorganisation. That would strengthen the report's own point that part of the gain is available without cutting hours.

**2. What do log-in hours include?**
The meetings mediation means different things depending on whether meeting time counts in the denominator.

- **If staff are logged in during meetings:** cutting meetings mechanically raises output per log hour. That is still a real gain, but it is accounting, not people working better.
- **If log time captures only active case work:** meetings are already outside the denominator. A 47% meetings share would then mean fewer meetings make case-work hours themselves more productive, for example through fewer interruptions and longer focus blocks. That is a more interesting and less obvious result.

The report should say which applies. The same question bears on what "stricter" means. Logs capture unclaimed case work, but they miss any work done outside the case system, in both arms.

**3. "Confirms" is stronger than the evidence supports.**
The summary says the mediation test "confirms" the meetings pathway. The body says it "survives a registered test," and the limitations note that mediation assumes no unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding. The body's wording is the right one.

The test is also not independent. It uses the same 14 offices in which the association was first noticed. Registering before the 24-month data reduces the comment's "post hoc" concern substantially, but it doesn't remove it.

The interval is a further question. A 28–66% interval from 14 clusters looks narrow. "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, not independent units. The report should say whether the mediation standard errors are clustered by office, with a small-cluster correction.

**4. Control-office meeting time needs reconciling.**
The control arm's average meeting time moved from 7.2 to 7.0 hours. The two audited offices alone fell by 2.1 hours each, which works out to about 0.6 hours across seven offices. That implies the other five rose by roughly 0.5 hours each. Weighting per person, or a different measurement window, might explain the gap, but it should be stated.

**5. Cost for the case-processing arm isn't reported.**
The report gives a cost estimate for the counter arm (+9% per contact) but none for case processing. Several things there carry costs:
- overtime;
- output per FTE of −3.4%;
- resignations of 4.1% against 7.9%, which saves recruitment and training.

For a county deciding whether to keep the scheme, cost per case closed is the number that matters.

**6. "Declined by about a quarter."**
On the like-for-like timesheet measure, the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% is about 22%. Comparing the 9-month timesheet figure (12.5%) with the 24-month log figure (8.5%) gives about 32%. Section 5 should name which comparison it means.

**Smaller point.** One of the three Halden reversions was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That stretches the discretionary/coverage binary: hard external deadlines behave partly like coverage. It supports the meta-analysis's limitation that the classification is coarse.

## Corrections to my own earlier reasoning

- **My meetings estimate was too high.** My back-of-envelope on the 9-month Varden data implied that roughly three-quarters of the per-hour gain came from fewer meetings. The registered estimate is 47%. My figure overstated the meetings share. It also implicitly assumed meeting time sat in the hours denominator, which is the open question in issue 2.
- **My survivorship concern was confirmed.** I suspected the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies leaned toward uncontrolled, scheduled-hours designs. The supplementary table shows they all were.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| Headline per-hour gains of more than 20% | **Explained.** They come from design and measurement. |
| "Entirely an artifact" | **Rejected.** About +8.5% per log hour at 24 months, randomised, with record-based output. |
| Durability | **Supported to 24 months, with some decline.** Part of the decline may be control-side catch-up (issue 1). Beyond 24 months is open. |
| Output per worker in discretionary work | **Roughly maintained, slightly below control** (−3.4%, with the CI including zero). Not shown to be equivalent. |
| Coverage-bound work | **Settled negative for this employer.** Waits rose, and restoring service costs about 9% more per contact. |
| Mechanism | **Partly resolved.** Meetings are the largest measured pathway (about half), fatigue is smaller (about a fifth), and about a third is unexplained. What meetings mean depends on what log hours include. |
| Can reorganisation alone capture the gain? | **Open, and now the most decision-relevant question.** Answering it needs an arm that reorganises without cutting hours, as the authors note. |

That last row is where I'd put the next study. A three-arm trial would separate the hours cut from the reorganisation it tends to trigger:
- reduced hours;
- a meeting and workflow audit at standard hours;
- control.
